# How to read this editorial

Two-pointer solutions are short, but the proof is the point. Every time a
pointer moves, ask:

> What candidates did we just discard, and why can none of them be part of a
> better answer?

For sliding windows, also ask why the left pointer never needs to move
backward. In this section, the reason is that all array values are
nonnegative.

# Problem A: Sorted Two Sum

## Restatement

Given a sorted array, determine whether two distinct elements sum to `k`.

## Important constraints and traps

The array is already sorted. You must use two distinct indices, so the loop
condition is `left < right`.

Values may be negative, but sorted two-sum still works because the array order
is monotone.

## Observations

Let `sum = a[left] + a[right]`.

- If `sum == k`, a pair exists.
- If `sum < k`, then `a[left]` is too small even with the largest available
  partner. Move `left` right.
- If `sum > k`, then `a[right]` is too large even with the smallest available
  partner. Move `right` left.

## Sample walk-through

Array:

```text
1 2 4 7 11
```

Target `9`.

| left | right | sum | action |
|---:|---:|---:|:---|
| 1 | 11 | 12 | move right |
| 1 | 7 | 8 | move left |
| 2 | 7 | 9 | found |

## Algorithm

```text
left = 0
right = n - 1
while left < right:
    total = a[left] + a[right]
    if total == k: YES
    if total < k: left += 1
    else: right -= 1
NO
```

## Correctness

At each step, all possible pairs using indices outside `[left, right]` have
already been safely discarded.

If `a[left] + a[right] < k`, then for every `j <= right`:

$$
a[left] + a[j] \le a[left] + a[right] < k.
$$

So `a[left]` cannot form a valid pair with any remaining element. Moving
`left` discards no solution.

If `a[left] + a[right] > k`, then for every `i >= left`:

$$
a[i] + a[right] \ge a[left] + a[right] > k.
$$

So `a[right]` cannot form a valid pair with any remaining element. Moving
`right` discards no solution.

If a valid pair exists, it remains inside the active range until it is found.
If the pointers cross, no pair remains. Therefore the algorithm is correct.

## Complexity

Each pointer moves at most `n` times. Time is `O(n)` and memory is `O(1)`.

## C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int T;
    cin >> T;
    while (T--) {
        int n;
        long long target;
        cin >> n >> target;
        vector<long long> values(n);
        for (long long &value : values) cin >> value;

        int left = 0;
        int right = n - 1;
        bool ok = false;
        while (left < right) {
            long long total = values[left] + values[right];
            if (total == target) {
                ok = true;
                break;
            }
            if (total < target) ++left;
            else --right;
        }
        cout << (ok ? "YES" : "NO") << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
```

## Python solution

```python
import sys


def exists_pair(values: list[int], target: int) -> bool:
    left = 0
    right = len(values) - 1
    while left < right:
        total = values[left] + values[right]
        if total == target:
            return True
        if total < target:
            left += 1
        else:
            right -= 1
    return False


data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
t = data[0]
idx = 1
out = []
for _ in range(t):
    n = data[idx]
    target = data[idx + 1]
    idx += 2
    values = data[idx:idx + n]
    idx += n
    out.append("YES" if exists_pair(values, target) else "NO")
sys.stdout.write("\n".join(out))
```

## Common wrong answers

- Using `left <= right`, which can use the same element twice.
- Moving the wrong pointer after comparing the sum.
- Forgetting duplicate values can form a valid pair if they are at distinct
  indices.

# Problem B: Longest Bounded Window

## Restatement

Find the maximum length of a contiguous subarray with sum at most `k`. Values
are nonnegative.

## Important constraints and traps

The empty subarray is allowed, so if every single value is greater than `k`,
the answer is `0`.

The nonnegative constraint is essential. Without it, this sliding-window
solution is not valid.

## Observations

Maintain a window `[left, right]` and its sum. Add each new `right` value. If
the sum becomes too large, move `left` right until the sum is valid again.

Because values are nonnegative, removing values from the left never increases
the sum.

## Sample walk-through

Array:

```text
2 1 3 4 2
```

Limit `7`.

| right | added | after shrinking | sum | best |
|---:|---:|:---|---:|---:|
| 0 | 2 | `[0,0]` | 2 | 1 |
| 1 | 1 | `[0,1]` | 3 | 2 |
| 2 | 3 | `[0,2]` | 6 | 3 |
| 3 | 4 | `[2,3]` | 7 | 3 |
| 4 | 2 | `[3,4]` | 6 | 3 |

## Algorithm

```text
left = 0
sum = 0
best = 0
for right from 0 to n - 1:
    sum += a[right]
    while sum > k:
        sum -= a[left]
        left += 1
    best = max(best, right - left + 1)
print best
```

## Correctness

After the shrinking loop finishes for a fixed `right`, the window sum is at
most `k`, so `[left, right]` is valid. Since values are nonnegative, any start
position smaller than `left` would include all elements of the current window
plus some removed nonnegative values; it cannot have smaller sum. Thus no
valid window ending at `right` starts before `left`.

Therefore `[left, right]` is the longest valid window ending at `right`.
Taking the maximum of these lengths over all `right` gives the longest valid
window overall.

## Complexity

Both pointers move only forward. Time is `O(n)` and memory is `O(1)`.

## C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int T;
    cin >> T;
    while (T--) {
        int n;
        long long limit;
        cin >> n >> limit;
        vector<long long> values(n);
        for (long long &value : values) cin >> value;

        int left = 0;
        long long total = 0;
        int best = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < n; ++right) {
            total += values[right];
            while (left <= right && total > limit) {
                total -= values[left];
                ++left;
            }
            best = max(best, right - left + 1);
        }
        cout << best << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
```

## Python solution

```python
import sys


def longest_window(values: list[int], limit: int) -> int:
    left = 0
    total = 0
    best = 0
    for right, value in enumerate(values):
        total += value
        while left <= right and total > limit:
            total -= values[left]
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best


data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
t = data[0]
idx = 1
out = []
for _ in range(t):
    n = data[idx]
    limit = data[idx + 1]
    idx += 2
    values = data[idx:idx + n]
    idx += n
    out.append(str(longest_window(values, limit)))
sys.stdout.write("\n".join(out))
```

## Common wrong answers

- Using `if total > k` instead of `while total > k`.
- Forgetting the answer can be zero.
- Applying this method to arrays with negative values.
- Updating `best` before shrinking to a valid window.

# Problem C: Count Subarrays At Most K

## Restatement

Count nonempty contiguous subarrays with sum at most `k`. Values are
nonnegative.

## Important constraints and traps

The answer may be `n(n+1)/2`, so use 64-bit integers in C++.

The task asks for count, not maximum length. For each right endpoint, many
subarrays may be valid.

## Observations

Use the same valid window `[left, right]` as in Problem B. After shrinking,
all starts from `left` through `right` form valid subarrays ending at `right`.

There are:

```text
right - left + 1
```

of them.

## Sample walk-through

Array:

```text
1 2 3
```

Limit `3`.

| right | valid starts | new subarrays | count |
|---:|:---|:---|---:|
| 0 | 0 | `[1]` | 1 |
| 1 | 0, 1 | `[1,2]`, `[2]` | 3 |
| 2 | 2 | `[3]` | 4 |

Answer: `4`.

## Algorithm

```text
left = 0
sum = 0
answer = 0
for right from 0 to n - 1:
    sum += a[right]
    while sum > k:
        sum -= a[left]
        left += 1
    answer += right - left + 1
print answer
```

## Correctness

After shrinking, `[left, right]` has sum at most `k`, and no window ending at
`right` with start before `left` is valid. Since values are nonnegative, any
subarray ending at `right` and starting at a position `s` with `left <= s <=
right` has sum no greater than the sum of `[left, right]`, so it is valid.

There are exactly `right - left + 1` such starts. The algorithm adds that
number, so it counts exactly all valid subarrays ending at `right`.

Every nonempty subarray has exactly one right endpoint. Summing the counts over
all right endpoints counts every valid subarray exactly once.

## Complexity

Each pointer moves at most `n` times. Time is `O(n)`, memory is `O(1)`.

## C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int T;
    cin >> T;
    while (T--) {
        int n;
        long long limit;
        cin >> n >> limit;
        vector<long long> values(n);
        for (long long &value : values) cin >> value;

        int left = 0;
        long long total = 0;
        long long answer = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < n; ++right) {
            total += values[right];
            while (left <= right && total > limit) {
                total -= values[left];
                ++left;
            }
            answer += right - left + 1;
        }
        cout << answer << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
```

## Python solution

```python
import sys


def count_subarrays(values: list[int], limit: int) -> int:
    left = 0
    total = 0
    answer = 0
    for right, value in enumerate(values):
        total += value
        while left <= right and total > limit:
            total -= values[left]
            left += 1
        answer += right - left + 1
    return answer


data = list(map(int, sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()))
t = data[0]
idx = 1
out = []
for _ in range(t):
    n = data[idx]
    limit = data[idx + 1]
    idx += 2
    values = data[idx:idx + n]
    idx += n
    out.append(str(count_subarrays(values, limit)))
sys.stdout.write("\n".join(out))
```

## Common wrong answers

- Adding only `1` for each valid right endpoint.
- Forgetting zero-valued elements create many valid subarrays.
- Using 32-bit `int` for the answer.
- Using this method with negative values.

# Stress testing strategy

All three problems have simple slow oracles:

- sorted two-sum: all pairs;
- longest bounded window: all subarrays, keep max valid length;
- count at most `k`: all subarrays, count valid ones.

The local random tests compare against these slow versions on small arrays.
Good tests include duplicates, zeros, limits of zero, all values too large,
and arrays where the shrinking loop runs many times.

# What to carry forward

Two-pointer algorithms are about monotonicity. A pointer move is justified only
when it discards candidates that cannot become useful later.

This idea will reappear in:

- binary search predicates;
- greedy algorithms;
- sweep-line active sets;
- offline query processing;
- advanced sliding-window counting problems.
